bucketA.title: Bucket A — Can CPD change or reorganize existing park identity?
bucketA.question: Does the Chicago Park District (or its predecessor bodies) have a track record of subdividing, reclassifying, consolidating, or redrawing the boundaries of existing park units?

items.title: South Park → Jackson Park + Washington Park + Midway Plaisance
items.whatHappened: In 1869–71 the South Park Commission created a single 1,055-acre park called 'South Park,' with an eastern division, western division, and connecting Midway. In 1880 the Commission solicited names for the divisions, and in 1881 formally named the eastern division Jackson Park and the western division Washington Park. CPD's own Midway Plaisance history states: 'All three sites were originally conceived as a single landscape known as South Park.' A 2022 CPD Board description says the original 1,055-acre complex is 'now home to modern-day Jackson Park, the Midway Plaisance, and Washington Park.' The National Park Service independently describes the same history.
items.whyItMatters: This is Jackson Park's own administrative lineage. The very park BBPAC is being told cannot be subdivided originated as a subdivision of a larger unified holding. Because this action predates CPD (it was the South Park Commission, absorbed into CPD in 1934), it should be framed as 'the administrative lineage from which Jackson Park arose demonstrates division is possible when geography, function, management and community use warrant it' — not as 'CPD already split Jackson Park before.' That distinction matters for legal precision.
items.verificationNote: Supported by CPD's own published park histories and corroborated independently by the National Park Service. Recommend pulling the primary CPD history-page text and NPS citation directly into the exhibit before external use.

items.title: Grant Park → Maggie Daley Park (a named park within a park)
items.whatHappened: CPD states that in 2014 it began transforming 'the northeastern part of Grant Park' into 'Maggie Daley Park' — described in CPD's capital-project record as 'a new multi-functional 27-acre park' replacing Daley Bicentennial Plaza and Peanut Park. CPD still refers to Maggie Daley as 'a park within Grant Park,' with its own name, programming, fieldhouse/operations, and supervisor identity. Internal capital ledgers place the project under Park No. 24 (Grant/Ulysses), completed 2015.
items.whyItMatters: This is CPD's cleanest modern (post-1934) reclassification action and establishes that CPD's park taxonomy is not binary (independent numbered park vs. mere facility) — there is a third category: a distinctly named, operationally recognizable 'park within a park.' This gives BBPAC a lower-friction alternative ask: designate a defined portion of Jackson Park as '63rd Street Bongo Beach Park,' a distinct park within Jackson Park for management, advisory and stewardship purposes — with park-number/PAC recognition sought separately.
items.verificationNote: Strong, current, and citable to CPD's own capital-project and history pages. Recommend obtaining the specific 2014–15 Board/administrative record establishing Maggie Daley's status (see Paper Trail item 5).

items.title: Lake Shore Playground → Lake Shore Park + Seneca Park (#1242)
items.whatHappened: CPD states that 'as early as 1907, the eastern portion of this park was considered part of nearby Lake Shore Playground.' In 1915 an armory physically separated the two park spaces; the City later treated the eastern parcel independently as Seneca Park, which CPD began leasing in 1959. Today Seneca is independently recorded as Seneca Park — Park No. 1242 (confirmed by CPD's capital records and the Chicago Public Library's CPD drawing archive). Lake Shore Park separately has its own Advisory Council; Seneca has its own park identity and PAC representation.
items.whyItMatters: This is the closest available example of land once treated as part of one park later being administered as its own separately numbered park with its own PAC. The limitation: the physical split was caused by the armory before CPD existed, not by an internal CPD Board decision — so this is strong evidence of the end-state BBPAC is asking for, but not proof CPD itself initiated an internal split.
items.verificationNote: Park #1242 identity is well-documented (CPL archive + a 2013 City lease exhibit citing 'Seneca Park-1242'). The original 1915–1959 administrative chain of custody still needs the underlying property/lease record (Paper Trail item 2).

items.title: Rutherford + Sayre + Rutherford Sayre → consolidated into Rutherford Sayre Park (#127)
items.whatHappened: CPD's own history describes three originally separate parks — Rutherford, Sayre, and Rutherford Sayre — that were combined by the Chicago Park District 'in mid-1999... to form Rutherford Sayre Park.'
items.whyItMatters: This is a modern, post-1934 CPD administrative restructuring of park identities — proof that CPD's internal park boundaries and identities are not historically frozen, and that CPD possesses the administrative authority to change the number/configuration of existing park units. It runs in the opposite direction from what BBPAC needs (consolidation, not division), but it directly supports the argument: 'if CPD can combine separately recognized park units into one, what rule prevents CPD from separating a sufficiently distinct portion of an oversized park into a distinct unit?' This is a fair question to put to CPD in writing, not a claimed entitlement.
items.verificationNote: The 1999 merger itself is stated in CPD's own park history. The underlying 1999 Board/administrative record, and which former park numbers were retired in the merger, are still unconfirmed (Paper Trail items 3–4) — do not assume specifics beyond what CPD has published.

items.title: CPD boundary transfers and additions (Dooley Park, Washington Park, 2024 Board actions)
items.whatHappened: CPD reports Dooley Park was expanded via a 1991 land acquisition, then in 2003 a portion was transferred to the City of Chicago for a Board of Education building. CPD reports Washington Park transferred roughly four acres for an armory in 1928 and another parcel to the Board of Education for Dyett High School in 1991. As recently as 2024, the CPD Board approved land transactions expressly to expand existing park boundaries.
items.whyItMatters: Establishes that park boundaries are administratively adjustable, not fixed cadastral lines — supporting evidence, not a standalone precedent for creating a new PAC-eligible unit.
items.verificationNote: Sourced to CPD's own published park histories and 2024 Board action reporting.

items.title: Northerly Island — Park No. 34 (downgraded as primary precedent)
items.whatHappened: CPD currently records Northerly Island as Park No. 34, and describes the former Meigs Field as transformed into a 119-acre park known as Northerly Island. However, Chicago Public Library's CPD archive has drawings labeled 'Northerly Island Park #34' dating to 1922 — meaning Park 34's separate identity predates modern CPD action.
items.whyItMatters: Good corroborating evidence that large lakefront park systems can include separately numbered park units, but it is not a clean modern 'split' precedent. Keep as supporting exhibit, not a lead argument.
items.verificationNote: Deliberately kept in the supporting-evidence tier per the source research — do not promote to a primary exhibit.

bucketB.title: Bucket B — Can a beach itself be an independent numbered CPD park?
bucketB.question: Does CPD's own park inventory show that a beach need not be administratively absorbed into a larger neighboring park?

items.title: Lane (George) Beach Park — Park #1265 (lead case)
items.whatHappened: CPD's history says the Lincoln Park Board once contemplated extending Lincoln Park north to Devon Avenue, but that extension never happened — Lincoln Park stopped at Ardmore Avenue in 1956. Lane Beach was acquired independently by CPD in the late 1950s and today is recognized as its own park: Lane (George) Beach Park, Park #1265 (confirmed by both CPD records and the Chicago Public Library's CPD drawing archive, with drawings dating to 1958). Lane is only 3.09 acres, yet CPD's data model treats Park #1265 as the parent property, with 'Lane Beach' and 'Lane Beach Playground' as facilities inside that separate park.
items.whyItMatters: This is the cleanest classification comparator: CPD's own inventory shows a small beach maintained as an independent numbered park (Park #1265 → Lane Beach, Lane Beach Playground) rather than folded into a much larger adjacent park. It does not prove CPD split Lane out of Lincoln Park (it did not), but it proves contiguity and common lakefront geography do not require a beach to share a larger neighboring park's administrative identity. The precise question to put to CPD: why is a substantially larger, more complex historic beach/environmental/cultural site (63rd Street Beach) classified only as a facility within Park #19, when a 3-acre beach elsewhere in the system carries its own park number?
items.verificationNote: Correctly labeled in the source research as 'Independent-beach-park precedent; not a proven CPD parcel-split precedent' — preserve that precise framing; do not overclaim it as a split precedent.

items.title: Chase Avenue Beach — Park #1250 (VOIDED) — separation candidate
items.whatHappened: CPD's history of Rogers Park and Beach says that by 1937 the larger Rogers Park and Beach property included lakefront/street-end beach areas at Chase Avenue, Greenleaf Avenue, and Farwell Avenue. CPD's official archival inventory separately recognizes 'Chase Avenue Beach — Park #1250,' identified as a voided property.
items.whyItMatters: This is the strongest available evidence resembling the pattern 'larger beach/park area → separately numbered beach property,' which is exactly the pattern BBPAC needs for 63rd Street Beach. The missing piece is the separation year and the Board/property-file action that created Park #1250 out of the larger Rogers Park holding — the source research deliberately does not invent that date.
items.verificationNote: Labeled 'SEPARATION CANDIDATE — YEAR REQUIRES BOARD/PROPERTY FILE' in the source research. This is a top-priority FOIA/archive target (see Evidence & Verification Status page).

items.title: Other standalone numbered Beach Parks (comparator set)
items.whatHappened: CPD's beach inventory includes numerous other beaches recognized as their own numbered parks, including Hartigan (David) Beach Park #1248, Doria (Helen) Beach Park #1251, Fargo (James) Beach Park #1253, Howard (Ure) Beach Park #1256, Mahony Griffin (Marion) Park #1257, Juneway Beach Park #1258, North Shore Beach Park #1260, Prinz (Tobey) Beach Park #1261, Rogers (Phillip) Beach Park #1262, and Leone (Sam) Beach Park #1013. For most of these, the source research found no documented split from a larger park.
items.whyItMatters: Reinforces that CPD's park inventory contains a large, well-established category of small independent beach parks — 63rd Street Beach's classification as a mere facility inside a 551-acre park is the outlier, not the norm, among CPD's own beaches.
items.verificationNote: Comparator list only — do not claim any of these were split from a larger park absent documentation. Rainbow Beach Park #1001 is the reverse case (a 1959 consolidation of two smaller municipal beaches, Rocky Ledge Beach and Rainbow Beach) — cite it accurately as a merger, not a split.

items.title: South Shore Beach vs. South Shore Cultural Center Park (#429) — an important non-precedent
items.whatHappened: South Shore Beach is not its own numbered park — it is a facility inside South Shore Cultural Center Park, Park #429. CPD purchased the former private South Shore Country Club property in 1974; the Chicago Public Library's Coalition archive says it was renamed South Shore Cultural Center Park in 1986. No evidence has been found that Park #429 was carved out of Jackson Park #19.
items.whyItMatters: South Shore is NOT direct evidence that CPD permits two PACs inside one park, and it is NOT a parcel-split precedent for 63rd Street Beach — the two beaches sit in different parent-park structures despite being geographically close. Its real value is as a comparator for what a dedicated, specialized lakefront PAC can accomplish (see the South Shore Cultural Center Advisory Council partner deck), not as a classification precedent.
items.verificationNote: Keep these two roles (comparator vs. precedent) strictly separate in every presentation — conflating them is the single easiest way to weaken the case's credibility with CPD's Planning or Law departments.

voidedProperties.note: See Chase Avenue Beach precedent above — separation candidate, year unconfirmed.

paperTrail.title: The Park-Number Administrative Paper Trail — 7 Questions
paperTrail.intro: Before leaning too heavily on any single precedent, the campaign needs the Park District's own park/property master record and its lifecycle history. These are the seven questions the FOIA/records campaign is built to answer. Status reflects what is proven from public sources today vs. what still requires CPD/CPL production — nothing below is guessed.

items.detail: CPD Board records expressly say CPD 'assigns an official park number to every property.' Park #543 was assigned when the City transferred the property in 2013; Park #581 was assigned when ownership transferred from the Board of Education in 2016. The underlying SOP/data manual has not been located publicly.

CPL's transferred CPD archive identifies 'Seneca Park (Park #1242).' A 2013 City lease exhibit identifies 'Seneca Park-1242,' 220–34 E. Chicago, including its PIN. The original assignment instrument itself is still not in hand.
CPD itself states the mid-1999 combination occurred, resulting in Rutherford Sayre Park #127. The dispositive 1999 Board/property record has not yet been produced.

items.target: Park numbers retired in the Rutherford/Sayre merger
items.detail: Deliberately unresolved — the source research does not guess the former numbers. Requires the 1999 property/database action.

Very strong administrative evidence: construction procurement called the project 'North Grant Park / Maggie Daley Park,' and CPD's capital ledger places 'Park development – Maggie Daley Park' under GRANT (ULYSSES), PARK NO. 24, completed 2015.

The parent property polygon is public (CPD_Parks, a MultiPolygon dataset with PARK_NO and GISOBJID). CPD_Facilities is only point geometry, so the public facility layer cannot establish the precise internal administrative sub-parcels around 63rd Street Beach.

items.target: Every Park Number split/merge/retirement/reassignment since 1934 ('the bullseye')
items.detail: This is the primary open investigation. CPL's transferred CPD drawing inventory expressly labels 53 Park Numbers 'voided property' — an initial seed universe, not proof of 53 splits/mergers. 'Voided' can mean consolidation, sale/disposition, transfer, abandoned acquisition, replacement, division, or administrative correction. The decisive production needed is the underlying park/property master database (active and inactive records) with status, creation/retirement dates, predecessor/successor numbers, and Board-action references, plus its audit trail.
